opus-5.5.text:
So, one way to think about it is this. Up until maybe 2020, it was the age of research. People were trying lots of different things, and the compute was small. Then from roughly 2020 to 2025, it was the age of scaling. Scaling laws and GPT-3 gave everyone a recipe: you take more data, more compute, a bigger network, and you get better results. That recipe was very attractive, especially for companies, because it's a low-risk way to invest resources. You know what you'll get.

But pre-training will run out of data. The data is finite. So the question becomes: what do you do next? Do you find some souped-up form of pre-training, or do you do RL, or something else entirely? Now that compute is so big, I think we're back in the age of research, just with very big computers.

On RL specifically, people are already spending more compute on it than on pre-training in some cases, because the rollouts are very long and each one gives you relatively little learning signal. So I'd ask whether that's even the most productive use of compute. "Scaling" has almost become a word people use without asking what they're scaling. The question isn't just how to make the number bigger. It's whether you've found the right thing to scale.

One thing I keep coming back to is generalization. These models generalize dramatically worse than people do. A model can do amazingly well on hard evals and then make some basic mistake, fix it, and reintroduce a previous bug. That disconnect is real, and I think it partly comes from how RL environments are chosen. People take inspiration from the evals, train on things that look like them, and then the model is like a student who practiced ten thousand hours for competitive programming. Very good at that, but not necessarily at the broader thing. So for me the most interesting direction isn't more RL of the same kind. It's understanding what's actually missing in generalization and what lets a human learn so much from so little. I think that's where the next leap comes from.

r001.rationale: It says rollouts are very long and each gives relatively little learning signal, explaining why RL can use more compute than pre-training.

r002.rationale: It asks whether RL is the most productive use of compute and says the key question is whether the right thing is being scaled.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention value functions or propose improving their use.

r004.rationale: It says we are back in an age of research and raises trying souped-up pre-training, RL, or something else.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the word "scaling" has done a lot of work for us, and maybe too much. For a while, the recipe was very simple: you have a fixed dataset, which is basically the internet, you make the model bigger, you make the compute bigger, and the loss goes down in a very predictable way. That was a gift. It meant you didn't have to be very clever. You just had to be disciplined.

Reinforcement learning is different in a way that I think people underappreciate. In pre-training, the data is given to you. In RL, the data is generated by the model itself, and then you have to decide what counts as good. So the thing you're scaling is no longer just parameters and tokens. You're scaling the quality of the signal. And the quality of the signal is not something you get for free by adding more GPUs. You get it by having environments that are actually rich, verifiers that are actually correct, and tasks where being good is not the same as being able to fool the grader.

So my view is that the clean scaling laws of pre-training will not transfer in the same form. You will see scaling, certainly. More compute in RL helps. Longer rollouts help. But the exponent is going to depend heavily on the environment, and I expect it to be much noisier and much more domain-specific. In mathematics and code, where you can check the answer, you'll see very fast progress. In domains where the reward is soft, it will be slower, and the failure modes will be stranger, because the model will find the gaps in your evaluation before you do.

The other thing I'd say is that RL puts the question of generalization back on the table. Pre-training gave the appearance of general intelligence because the data was so broad. With RL, you can train a model to be extraordinary at a narrow thing and it may or may not carry over. Whether it carries over is, to me, the real research question of the next few years. Not "how much compute," but "does getting better at this make you better at that." If the answer is yes, then scaling RL is the whole story. If the answer is mostly no, then we're going to have to rediscover some ideas that got set aside when pre-training was working so well.

r001.rationale: The response says RL can benefit from more compute and longer rollouts, but does not identify small learning gains per rollout as a reason RL consumes large amounts of compute.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes reward-signal quality and generalization, but does not propose comparing training approaches by how productively they use compute.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention value functions or their potential to improve compute efficiency.

r004.rationale: It says researchers may need to rediscover sidelined ideas, but does not clearly predict exploratory experimentation with different training approaches.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing to ask is: what exactly are we scaling? With pre-training, the answer was quite clear. You had more data, a larger model, more compute. And you had a fairly reliable relationship between those inputs and the result.

With reinforcement learning, you can spend more compute, but you also need to specify what the model is learning from. What are the tasks? How do you determine whether it did well? Is it discovering something new, or becoming very good at a narrow set of problems?

So the question becomes how to build a training process where additional compute keeps producing useful learning. If the model has exhausted what it can learn from an environment, running it for longer may not help very much. You need richer problems, or some way for the difficulty to grow with the model’s ability.

And then there is generalization. You can get a very impressive result on the thing you reward. But how much does that improve the model’s ability to handle a situation that you didn’t anticipate? I think that is a central question. Scaling still matters, but the recipe determines what you get when you scale.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether more compute yields useful learning, but does not identify the small amount of learning per rollout as a reason RL can consume large amounts of compute.

r002.rationale: It says to build a training process where additional compute keeps producing useful learning, making compute productivity the criterion for judging the approach.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention value functions or suggest using them to improve compute efficiency.

r004.rationale: The response does not predict a return to exploratory experimentation with different training approaches.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to distinguish scaling a method from discovering what to scale. With pre-training, we found a recipe where more compute, more data, and larger models produced fairly predictable improvements. That was an unusually simple situation.

With reinforcement learning, you can spend more compute, but the question is: doing what? What environments are you learning in? How good is the feedback? Is the model discovering something new, or becoming very good at the particular tasks you can measure?

So I would expect compute to remain very important. But I wouldn’t assume that the predictability of pre-training automatically carries over. You need a learning process that turns additional computation into capabilities that generalize. Finding that process is a research problem. Once you have it, scaling becomes powerful again.

r001.rationale: It discusses compute and feedback, but does not identify limited learning per rollout as a reason RL can consume large amounts of compute.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes whether additional computation produces generalizing capabilities, framing productive use of compute as the key question.

r003.rationale: It does not mention value functions or suggest improving their use.

r004.rationale: It calls finding a scalable learning process a research problem, but does not predict exploratory experimentation with different training approaches.
